title: The cubical open-box pair homeomorphism
statement: Let $I=[0,1]$ with its usual topology. For $n\geq0$, give $I^n$ its product topology and put $\partial I^n=\{u\in I^n:\text{some coordinate of }u\text{ equals }0\text{ or }1\}$; thus $I^0$ is a point and $\partial I^0=\varnothing$. Set $J_n=(\partial I^n\times I)\cup(I^n\times\{0\})\subset I^n\times I$. Every displayed subset is equipped with its subspace topology [def-kun-subspace-topology]. There exists a homeomorphism $h_n:I^n\times I\to I^n\times I$ such that $h_n(I^n\times\{0\})=J_n$. Equivalently, the pairs $(I^n\times I,I^n\times\{0\})$ and $(I^n\times I,J_n)$ are homeomorphic. A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. A homeomorphism of pairs means a homeomorphism of the ambient spaces carrying the specified subspace onto the specified subspace; no pointwise fixing of that subspace is asserted.

proof.text: For n=0, I^0 is a point and J_0=I^0×{0}; the identity of I is the required homeomorphism. The subspace topology used for J_0 is the induced topology of [def-kun-subspace-topology].

source.place: Lemma 2.4.13 proof, printed p. 55 (the n=0 case).

proof.text: Assume $n>0$. In the square $Q=[0,1]^2$ set $A=(0,0)$, $P=(1/2,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(1,1)$, $D=(0,1)$, $E=(1/2,1)$ and $O=(1/2,1/2)$. The five closed triangles with vertex triples $(O,A,P),(O,P,B),(O,B,C),(O,C,D),(O,D,A)$ cover $Q$ with disjoint interiors. Define $F:Q\to Q$ by the affine vertex correspondence $(O,A,P,B,C,D)\mapsto(O,A,B,C,E,D)$ on these triangles. Their images are the five triangles $(O,A,B),(O,B,C),(O,C,E),(O,E,D),(O,D,A)$, which also cover $Q$ with disjoint interiors. Every triangle on both lists is nondegenerate. The affine pieces and their affine inverses agree on shared edges, since there they have the same endpoint values. Thus they define mutually inverse continuous maps: for any closed set its preimage is the finite union of its closed preimages in the closed triangles. In particular $F$ is a homeomorphism, with inverse $G$ given by the reversed vertex correspondence.

proof.text: On the left edge $DA$, $F$ is the identity because both endpoints are fixed. On the bottom edge, its two affine pieces give $F(r,0)=(2r,0)$ for $0\le r\le1/2$ and $F(r,0)=(1,2r-1)$ for $1/2\le r\le1$. Consequently $F$ sends the bottom edge onto the bottom-and-right edge union. Write $F(r,t)=(R(r,t),T(r,t))$ and $G(s,v)=(\rho(s,v),\tau(s,v))$. Both maps fix the left edge pointwise; since they are inverse bijections, $r>0$ implies $R(r,t)>0$, and $s>0$ implies $\rho(s,v)>0$.

proof.text: The radius functions are continuous finite maxima, so the displayed quotient formulas prove continuity of $H$ and $K$ away from their central axes. At $(0,t_0)$, continuity of $F$ and $F(0,t_0)=(0,t_0)$ give $R(r(x),t)\to0$ and $T(r(x),t)\to t_0$ as $(x,t)\to(0,t_0)$. Every spatial output coordinate of $H$ has absolute value at most $R(r(x),t)$, which proves continuity there. At $(0,v_0)$, continuity of $G$ and $G(0,v_0)=(0,v_0)$ give $\rho(s(y),v)\to0$ and $\tau(s(y),v)\to v_0$; the spatial coordinates of $K$ have absolute value at most $\rho(s(y),v)$, so $K$ is continuous there as well. Thus $H$ and $K$ are inverse homeomorphisms.

source.place: Lemma 2.4.13 proof, printed p. 55: explicit agent expansion of the cubical side-flattening construction.

proof.text: The bottom-edge formulas give $H(x,0)=(2x,0)$ when $r(x)\le1/2$, and $H(x,0)=(x/r(x),2r(x)-1)$ when $r(x)\ge1/2$. The first branch covers $C_n\times\{0\}$: $(y,0)$ is the image of $(y/2,0)$. The second branch covers $\partial C_n\times I$, where $\partial C_n=\{y:r(y)=1\}$: $(y,v)$ is the image of $(((v+1)/2)y,0)$. Hence $H(C_n\times\{0\})=(C_n\times\{0\})\cup(\partial C_n\times I)$. With the coordinatewise affine homeomorphism $a:I^n\to C_n$, $a(u)_i=2u_i-1$, define $h_n=(a^{-1}\times\operatorname{id}_I)\circ H\circ(a\times\operatorname{id}_I)$. The equation $r(a(u))=1$ is equivalent to some $u_i$ being $0$ or $1$, the map $a\times\operatorname{id}_I$ sends $I^n\times\{0\}$ onto $C_n\times\{0\}$, and $a^{-1}\times\operatorname{id}_I$ sends the centered bottom-and-sides union onto $J_n$. Therefore $h_n(I^n\times\{0\})=J_n$. Restricting $h_n$ and its inverse to these subsets is continuous for their induced topologies [def-kun-subspace-topology]: an open set in a subset is an ambient open set intersected with the subset, and its preimage has the same form. This proves the asserted homeomorphism of pairs.
